title: Is Anybody Out There?
blurb: Nobody has ever found an alien. This is the true story of how hard people are looking, and what they would accept as proof.

1.title: Is Anybody Out There?
1.subtitle: A read-together story for ages 3 to 4
1.intro: Read this story out loud together. Point to the picture as you go.

blocks.prompt: Look at the picture. Wave back at the alien.

notes: Nobody has found a real one yet
People look with big telescopes

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: Look up at the night sky. Do you see the little lights? Each light is a star. Some stars have planets going around them, just like our Earth goes around the sun. Nobody knows if anyone lives out there. People point big telescopes at the sky and listen. They are looking for a friend. Maybe one day we will find one.

2.title: Is Anybody Out There?
2.subtitle: A reading sheet for ages 5 to 6
2.intro: Read the story. Then do each part.

blocks.prompt: Read the story, then answer the questions. Take your time.

notes: A planet at another star is called an exoplanet

blocks.prompt: The Planets We Have Never Visited
blocks.text: Earth is not the only planet. Scientists have found thousands of other planets going around other stars. They call them exoplanets. Some are hot balls of gas. Some are frozen rocks. A few are just the right warmth for water to stay liquid, and water is what life on Earth needs most. So far, nobody has found life on any of them. Not a plant. Not a bug. Not a person. But we have only looked at a tiny piece of the sky. There are more stars out there than there are grains of sand on every beach on Earth.

water

3.title: Is Anybody Out There?
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: SETI means the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence
Frank Drake started listening in 1960
The Wow signal lasted 72 seconds
It has never been heard again

blocks.prompt: The Word in the Margin
blocks.text: For most of history, people could only guess whether anyone else was out there. Then we built radios. In 1960, an astronomer named Frank Drake pointed a radio telescope at two nearby stars and listened for a signal. He heard nothing unusual, but he had started something. Ever since, scientists have kept listening. This search has a name. It is called SETI, which stands for the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence. The idea is simple. If another civilization builds radios, their signals might leak out into space, and one of our dishes might catch one. In 1977, a telescope in Ohio picked up a strong, strange burst of radio noise that lasted 72 seconds. The astronomer who found it in the printout circled it and wrote one word in the margin: Wow. Nobody has ever heard that signal again, and nobody has explained it. That is where the search stands. We have listened for more than sixty years, and the sky has stayed quiet.

4.title: Is Anybody Out There?
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Extremophiles are living things that survive extremes
Europa hides an ocean under its ice
Enceladus sprays water into space
Cassini flew through the spray and found organics
Tidal heating warms a moon from the inside
Most scientists expect microbes, not people

blocks.prompt: Not Little Green Men. Microbes.
blocks.text: When people imagine aliens, they picture something like us: two eyes, two legs, a spaceship. Scientists searching for life expect something far humbler. They are hunting for microbes. Here is why that search has gotten serious. For a long time, biologists assumed life needed mild conditions. Then they started finding organisms in places that should have been lethal. There are bacteria living in near boiling water at deep sea vents, in acid, inside rock miles underground, and in the cooling ponds of nuclear reactors. Scientists call them extremophiles, which means lovers of extremes. Every one of them widened the map of where life could survive. That map now includes moons. Europa circles Jupiter under a shell of ice, and beneath that ice is a salty ocean that may hold more water than every ocean on Earth combined. Enceladus, a small moon of Saturn, sprays plumes of water from cracks near its south pole. A spacecraft named Cassini flew straight through one of those plumes and found salt, and organic molecules, and hydrogen gas. Hydrogen is food for certain bacteria on Earth. Neither moon sits in what astronomers call the habitable zone, the ring around a star where sunlight keeps water liquid. Both are far too distant for that. They stay warm a different way. Jupiter and Saturn squeeze and stretch them with gravity, and the flexing generates heat from the inside. Nobody has found a single cell out there yet. But the question has changed. It used to be whether liquid water existed anywhere else. It does. Now the question is whether water plus warmth plus time is enough.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in full sentences.
items: What are scientists actually hunting for, and how is that different from what most people imagine?

The passage says the question has changed. What was the old question, and what is the new one?
answers: microbes; most people imagine something like us with eyes, legs, and a spaceship
life survives extremes, so cold and dark places like moons became worth searching
gravity from Jupiter and Saturn squeezes and stretches them, and the flexing makes heat inside
old: does liquid water exist anywhere else; new: is water plus warmth plus time enough for life

5.title: Is Anybody Out There?
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The Drake equation was written in 1961
It organizes a question, it does not answer one
In 1961 we knew of zero exoplanets
Enrico Fermi asked: where is everybody
Life starting is a sample of one
The searched sky is a glass out of an ocean

blocks.prompt: Where Is Everybody?
blocks.text: In 1961, a year after his first search came up empty, Frank Drake sat down to write an agenda for a small meeting. What he wrote instead became the most famous equation in the search for life. The Drake equation does not calculate an answer. It organizes a question. To estimate how many communicating civilizations exist in our galaxy right now, Drake argued, you multiply seven things together: how often stars form, what fraction have planets, how many of those planets could support life, how often life actually starts, how often life becomes intelligent, how often intelligence builds something that broadcasts, and, last and worst, how long such a civilization lasts before it goes silent. The first three terms have improved enormously. In 1961 we knew of no planets outside our solar system. We now know of more than five thousand, and the evidence suggests that planets are the rule, not the exception. Every one of those numbers has moved in a hopeful direction. The last four remain guesses. Nobody knows how hard it is for chemistry to become biology, because it has happened, as far as we can prove, exactly once. A sample of one supports no statistics at all. Which brings us to the problem the physicist Enrico Fermi is said to have raised over lunch in 1950. The galaxy is about thirteen billion years old. Even at speeds we could build today, a patient civilization could cross it in a few million years, which is a blink at that scale. So, Fermi asked, where is everybody? Explanations are cheap and evidence is scarce. Maybe life is vanishingly rare. Maybe intelligence is rare. Maybe civilizations reliably destroy themselves. Maybe they are out there and quiet, or out there and unrecognizable, or out there and simply not interested in us. Maybe we have not looked long enough or hard enough, which is worth remembering. The total amount of sky that SETI has searched carefully is often compared to scooping a single glass of water out of the ocean and concluding there are no fish.

(inform, with detail: it defines the equation and gives dates and facts; it argues gently at the end)
(we have barely searched, so silence is not evidence of absence)

6.title: Is Anybody Out There?
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Transmission spectroscopy reads a planet's air from starlight
A biosignature is a gas biology makes and geology does not
Earth's air is about 21 percent oxygen, nearly all of it exhaled by life
Oxygen alone can be faked by a lifeless planet
The 1967 pulsar was first labeled LGM-1, for Little Green Men
Technosignatures hunt for technology, not biology

blocks.prompt: How We Would Actually Know
blocks.text: Suppose there is life on a planet orbiting another star. How would we ever find out? We cannot go. The nearest star beyond our sun is more than four light years away, which means our fastest spacecraft would need tens of thousands of years to arrive. Whatever we learn, we will learn from light. That constraint is less crippling than it sounds. When a planet passes in front of its star, a sliver of starlight filters through the planet's atmosphere before it reaches us. Different gases absorb different wavelengths, so the light arrives with a barcode of missing lines. Read the barcode and you have read the air of a world you will never visit. The James Webb Space Telescope does this now, and has detected water vapor, carbon dioxide, and methane in the atmospheres of distant planets. The hope is to find a biosignature: a gas that biology makes and geology does not. Oxygen is the classic candidate. Earth's atmosphere is about twenty one percent oxygen, and essentially all of it was exhaled by living things over billions of years. Left alone, oxygen reacts with rock and disappears. Finding it in quantity would mean something is topping it up. The trouble is that nature is a forger. Astronomers have worked out several ways a lifeless planet can accumulate oxygen, mainly by having its water broken apart by starlight while the light hydrogen escapes to space. So a single gas proves nothing. What convinces is a combination that should not coexist: oxygen and methane together, for instance, since they destroy each other and must both be constantly replenished. The cautionary tale is recent. In 2020, a team announced phosphine in the clouds of Venus, a gas that on Earth is associated with life. The finding was reported everywhere and is still disputed. Reanalysis weakened the signal, other groups failed to confirm it, and possible non biological sources were proposed. Nobody committed fraud. The claim was simply harder than it first appeared, which is the normal condition of frontier science. There is an older cautionary tale too. In 1967, Jocelyn Bell Burnell found a radio source pulsing with impossible regularity, roughly once every 1.3 seconds. The team labeled it LGM-1, for Little Green Men, half joking and half not. It turned out to be a pulsar: a collapsed star spinning and sweeping a beam past us like a lighthouse. The universe, it turns out, makes rhythm without help. So the search continues on two tracks. Biosignatures hunt for life of any kind, including pond scum. Technosignatures hunt for the products of technology: radio broadcasts, laser pulses, waste heat, industrial pollution in an atmosphere. Both are searches for something we have never seen, which makes them scientifically awkward. You cannot fully specify what you are looking for. And yet the asymmetry is enormous. Sixty years of silence has taught us relatively little, because the sky is large and our attention has been narrow. But a single confirmed detection would be among the most consequential facts ever established. That imbalance is the whole argument for looking. Not because we expect to succeed, but because the payoff for succeeding is so extreme that even a small chance is worth the price of a few telescopes.
